i’m a nurse on a cardiac floor but disclaimer i’m not giving you medical advice just my opinion. 

1. your heart rate is fine unless you are symptomatic, think dizzy or loss of consciousness

2. i forget what maximum heart rate is supposed to be for age, but if it’s too high just slow down when running it’s not a sign of disease if it gets to 180 when running, you might just be going too fast

3.  cardiac pain is not reproducible, meaning you can’t touch it and make it worse. it will get worse on exertion and usually not go away while exerting yourself and usually you would get other symptoms of a heart attack if you keep exerting yourself to pair with the pain like nausea and vomiting. if this is the case then you would need a stress test (answer to #5 as well because the test you see in movies is a stress test and this only needs to be done if they suspect a blockage)

4. in my experience, if the pain was cardiac pain it wouldn’t go away while you continue to exert yourself, it would get worse and result in a heart attack. this seems muscular.

5. see answer #3

6. it’s most likely exertional effort that’s causing your heart rate to be higher

7. again i think it’s how you are exerting yourself. slow down. 

8. you may need anxiety meds or something lol, this seems excessive. not trying to be mean but if this continues to consume you to where you are seeing several doctors for what seems like normal things then it may be a hyperfixation problem. if it ends up being an actual problem then ignore my anxiety suggestion.

i was t-boned by a drunk driver, woke up in the hospital, spent about a week there and then about a month in bed at home recovering. tbi, fractured skull, leg, five vertebrae, ribs, busted eardrum, cuts everywhere, my organs were fucked, bruised and swollen all over. i was already depressed to begin with because i was kicked out of the military after basic training for reasons that haven’t been relevant to my life for about ten years. and about a month after that, the girl i was planning on marrying dumped me because i was now a loser delivering pizza, and living with my parents. 
i was pretty fucked up. 
i vividly remember laying in the guest bedroom on the first floor, because i couldn’t make it up the stairs to my bedroom. it was dark, everything hurt, i could barely move, and my mom walked in to check on me. the painkillers they gave me never really worked, and i was just frustrated. i remember crying to my mom like a baby, and feeling like i was scraping the bottom.  
honestly i don’t know why, but as soon as i was able to, i started doing little workouts in the garage. 
i was slowly shuffling around the house like a thousand year old man, and doing things like knee pushups, and dips with my walker while wearing my back brace. i looked ridiculous lol 
i spent about seven months prior to basic training exercising with a group to prepare for that, and the schools we’d go to after. so i guess after that stuff, i was just kind of conditioned mentally, and exercising was what i was programmed to do.
eventually i started running again, with an intense pain in my leg. my mom said i was being a wuss and to push through it. i eventually insisted on having it looked at. evidently the hospital i was transported to missed a fractured fibula, but by the time i got the x-ray, the bones had already fused back together. so i guess mom was right, i had nothing to complain about. 
one day while laying in bed wallowing, feeling sorry for myself, and thinking about just ending it all, i thought “i’m sick of this being my life. either i’m going to kill myself, or i’m not.” so i decided against it. my reasoning being... curiosity. i just wanted to see what else would happen (probably the brain damage talking lol). 
so, i just kind of started peeling myself out of bed to go on runs, do workouts in the garage, and go lift weights at the gym. 
thanks to my persist rehabilitation efforts, i was cleared to go back to work early by my doctor. 
i had about... eight months as a volunteer firefighter before the accident (timeline is fuzzy, this was all a while ago, sorry) and finally got back to work. 
i went back to school and got my emt certification and started applying for paid departments. 
i met a girl, we spent a lot of time together, we took a trip to a national park, and on the way there we drove through a city she had lived in and i had always wanted to visit. i loved it. 
i got a paid job at a fire department near her and my parents. it turned out to be possibly the single most poorly run organization i’ve ever seen in my life. but i learned a lot and got some experience. 
she had applied to the university at that city we passed through, and was accepted. 
two months after we started seeing each other, she asked if i wanted to come and i said absolutely. 
i started applying for departments there, drove a lot, lots of paperwork, lots of tests, and finally got a job just outside the city. we moved, i worked, i proposed and she said yes, a year later we moved to a better part of the city, we got a puppy... 
now we’re here, i’m strong, i’m healthy, i’m capable, i live in a city i love, i love my job, i love our dog, our cats... i love my life. i’m on an antidepressant and seeing a counselor every other week (which evidently i desperately needed both and was nearly forced to talk to someone by my fiancée), but i’m genuinely the happiest i have ever been in my entire life. 
life is hard, but i finally understand the good and bad go hand in hand, and that’s just how life is. it’s a bike ride in 104° late afternoon heat with your legs cramping up, out of water, exhausted, but the wind is blowing, everything around you is beautiful, and when you’re done you stop at a shit hole gas station and grab all the drinks and snacks you want and just let your brain bask in the oxygenated pool of endorphins. then go home, jump into a pool, enjoy the company of people and animals that love you...

i think this article is an important part of the discussion about health and well-being. the author discusses how running started out as a boon in her life, and clearly details how it becomes harmful: running to the point of illness or injury, suffering panic attacks if she couldn’t run, and derailing relationships in order to keep running. it becomes an activity that begins causing her distress and negatively impacts her life, but she continues to do it, because she feels she must.

she isn’t saying that being dedicated to running is inherently bad. she’s not saying that running or exercising often is inherently bad. she’s saying that it is possible for these behaviors to become more harmful than helpful, and turn into a disordered activity.

she’s not saying people shouldn’t work out. she’s saying that people need to be aware that there is an edge over which they can fall. not that every body or even most people will cross that line, but that the line exists.

and the author highlights a particular struggle with identifying this type of disordered behavior: people view exercise as wholly healthful, so determining when it becomes a problem or even having it recognized as a problem can be challenging.

i think it’s a good article, and that the author’s experience isn’t meant to be applied to everybody’s personal relationship to running.

so i've had some wicked pain in my lower back for about 5 years now that really seemed like it was spinal stenosis.  the pain would build up as i walked but relieved when i sat down.  going up hills or leaning on a shopping cart helped.  plus, apparently this runs in my family.  great, off to a neurosurgeon who agreed it sounded pretty cut and dry, ordered me off for an mri aaaaannnnnnddddd... 

no spinal stenosis.  i have a slightly dehydrated disk that shouldn't be an issue until i'm 70 and i might want to check with a vascular surgeon since there's a artery condition that could potentially mimic spinal stenosis.  by the time i got to the neurosurgeon i'd already been at this for about 3 years with lots of different physical therapy and whatnot.

so last year it's off to the vascular surgeon who orders some tests and nope, everything is perfect.  he suggests i go back to a neurologist.  so i do that and he can't think of anything else and tells me i need to go to a sports doctor.  sport doctors in the netherlands deal with sports injuries and the injuries that prevent active people from staying active (more unusual cases that a normal fysio can't figure out).  she did a few tests and told me that my glutes were inactive and my stabilization muscles were weak.  this is probably the root of it all and she sent me off to two physical therapists that specialize in more severe and weird cases.  one is a manual therapist and the other is the actual pt for exercises.

i was skeptical of their diagnosis at first because i was deadlifting 180kg, hiking all over, etc.  how could my glutes be inactive?  however, it turns out that everything else has been doing what they are supposed to do and what the glutes are supposed to do leaving my glutes and stabilization muscles pretty damned weak and inactive.  it's actually working and it's sloooooooooowly getting better after 6 months (and probably have 6-8 months or more to go).

i guess the point i'm trying to make is you have to keep at it looking for answers.  maybe an equivalent of a sports doctor can help? maybe different physical therapists? maybe a sports therapist?  good luck, i know how frustrating chronic pain like this is.

>that there's an assumption that to be healthy you need to count calories.

i would say you're unpacking it too many steps. 

to reach specific physical goals - be it weight, physique, strength - calorie counting is a useful tool to get there efficiently and without damaging your body. 

it's helpful to think of fitness as a hobby. it is ok to make fitness a hobby. many people make fitness a hobby because it is healthy. it can even be healthy to have fitness as a hobby, but not necessarily so. health itself may not necessarily be the goal, although it can be a motivator and a nice bonus. 

you're right, many people who are already 'healthy' have goals that they are counting calories to help them achieve. and even when their goals are healthy, while it might make them healthier in the long run, the goal itself still is not necessarily connected to health. a healthy person dropping 5 kilo wants something else, maybe to fit into an old dress or to feel better about themselves naked. a healthy person trying to get some arm muscles might want to be stronger so she can pick up her kids or to have a gun show to flash on a whim. i would argue that they are getting healthier, but for reasons that are unconnected to health. 

conversely, lots of people take their goals and their calorie counting to extremes. i think we can agree this is often problematic. people can have a goal of reaching an unrealistic weight, of reaching an unrealistic physique, of cutting an unhealthy level of calories. they may have started because it's healthy, but in the end, they are actually making unhealthy choices and possibly damaging their bodies.

recovering from bed right now. three things that have helped me, specifically with running: 

1) getting lots of protein helps. a protein shake right after a run helped me keep on track for meals for the rest of the day.

2) make yourself a long-term running plan, like a 16-week 10km or half-marathon training plan (depending on where your fitness goals are at right now). even if you’re not training for an actual race, having the long term plan will help you both a) have running goals completely unrelated to your food, and b) give you a damn good reason to do the short run on short run day even though you binged the night before because, dammit, it says right here on my training plan that i’m only going for a short run today! (lol)

3) try to mentally separate your running goals from your food goals. this one takes a lot lot lot of self-talk, and i’m only seeing success with it after months of therapy for bed. an example of something that has worked for me is asking myself before i do any form of exercise “am i excited about doing this?” if the answer is no, or if the answer is “yes but i also need to push hard to punish”, i either don’t go, or i challenge myself to stay in a lower heart rate zone, or remind myself that i have permission to walk whenever and how ever many times i feel like it in my run. we run to feel good, because we love the endorphins. the second it becomes about punishment, force yourself to stop, slow down, wait until you feel excited again. force through the embarrassment of “if people see me walking they’ll judge me” or whatever else is going on in your brain. self-talk is hard, but it’s really key.

i’m an ent, so i deal with this often. here’s what i tell my patients:

1.	nasal saline irrigations (neilmed irrigation bottle is what i give to patients, but navage and other powered devices work well too) after you run and before any intranasal sprays (flonase, rhinocort, nasonex, astepro, astelin, etc.). this cleans out your sinuses, manually rinsing away aeroallergens. 
2.	first line for congestion: intranasal corticosteroids. i take flonase personally and it is what i most frequently prescribe. if you have a lot of sneezing, i find astelin (intranasal antihistamine) to be very effective at mitigating that symptom in particular. 
3.	oral antihistamines. second generation medications (zyrtec, allegra, xyzal) have relatively few side effects and good efficacy for allergic rhinitis. most common side effect is drowsiness. if one makes you drowsy, try a different one. 
4.	some patients, especially those with asthma and type 2-mediated/ectopic disease get a fair amount of benefit from the addition of singulair on top of these other medications. there is a black box warning on singulair for risk of increased suicidal thoughts. 
5.	some people (myself included) get a lot of nasal drainage from exercise-induced non-allergic rhinitis, or vasomotor rhinitis. if you have copious, clear, watery nasal drainage that’s exacerbated by running, this could be you. this often responds well to anticholinergic nose sprays like atrovent, but i believe is prescription only. 

tl;dr: nasal saline irrigations, flonase, zyrtec are a must. astelin, singulair, atrovent are helpful for some. if you’re taking multiple medications and still having breakthrough symptoms, consult your pcp or local ent for consideration of allergy testing and immunotherapy. 

legal disclaimer: this is not prescriptive medical advice, but simply a generally accepted pathway for medical management of allergy in the ent world. ask your doctor before starting/stopping any medications.

former hs girl tennis player here who (wearily) weathered 4 years of drama. not to scare you, but it made me stop playing for about 5 years; i recently picked it up again through usta toc in grad school and it has been exponentially more enjoyable. 

in my experience, do you best to be to not play favorites. 

if the goal of the team is to win matches or sectionals, or go to state, etc., then set up your lineup using a ladder with challenge matches so that the girls can clearly see where they should be and it’s not on you to “make the call.” that also lets them have an avenue to focus on improvement - they know they can challenge and what the requirements are to do so. 

however, if the goal of your season is to “show improvement” for all players, then the team needs to know this, be on board, and agree to support each other.

sending mixed messages about team goals is a death sentence, because it causes anxiety in the less strong players and creates a place for people to complain about their partners letting them down. i’ve been on both sides, even in college, and this is always terrible. 

also, if you’re trying to set up doubles partners, you could try an old trick from a teacher friend- have everyone submit a favorite partner and a least favorite partner to you confidentially. this can be redone a couple times as the season progresses/things change. that gives you a starting point, an insight into any potential problems, and lets you get a feel for how each player views their abilities in relation to others on the team. girls especially know exactly where they think they should be. it’s your job as coach to put those expectations in context, but this gives you a good starting point for both relationships and for perceived tennis ability.

i'm not op, but i did fully recover from an eating disorder that involved binging and calorie counting and now eat 100% intuitively.

the way i made the transition was, like op said, not tracking at all. but i borrowed overeater's anonymous's and my ed counselor's advice for what "sane" eating looks like and kept a food journal.

basically, to consider yourself "on track" sans calorie counting, you eat 3 meals a day with no snacks. each meal should contain just enough food to get you to the next meal without starving. your plate should generally be 50% vegetable matter, 25% protein, and 25% starch. if you find yourself needing to snack, eat bigger meals. sugar is not a food; don't eat desserts most days.

by doing this, i achieved intuitive eating and a slim figure that feels effortless thanks to it being habit and not a weight loss attempt. if you view it as a weight loss attempt it's more exhausting i think.

do this long enough and it will sink in eventually. 6 months. a year. then for the rest of your life.

somedays i have to pinch myself because i still can't believe i lost the weight obsession after so many years of struggling. i suffered hardcore for 4 years, then spent another 4 years on a relapse roller coaster which ended when i got very serious about this plan. 

also, cook for yourself from scratch like 2-5 days/week.

what got me out of the rut was actually a couple of things...

1. i decided that i was bored with my routine. i had been going into the gym and predominately doing different variations of the same lifts for 12+ years. i joined a club hiit gym. this is the most important part. i changed my routine completely. it was something new, even down to the environment. it made it seem a little more exciting.

3. these workouts are instructor-led. so there’s really no cheating or skipping exercises. the whole class will be doing the movements and it helps me not slack off.

i know this isn’t financially practical for everyone. these kinds of gyms/classes tend not to be cheap. but if you can afford it, having something like this that is led by someone else and is scheduled at specific times can lead to more consistency and commitment. a trainer would be a good option as well because it also involves scheduling and commitment.

try to set up a mechanism that puts workouts more rigidly into your schedule: even if it’s setting a workout time with a friend. i found that what really worked for me was this mix of scheduling and financial commitment.

i agree that megyn kelly is not being nice in this situation; she has a blunt, sometimes confrontational style that can be off-putting (speaking mildly) or demeaning (speaking harshly).  though imo it is fair game to point out osaka's statements and actions appear to be contradictory, kelly lowered herself by engaging in a war of words on twitter.  that's not the real issue though.  the real issue is a) naomi osaka has essentially said she is shy and does not want the attention and scrutiny associated with being a high profile tennis player but also b) osaka *chose* to take an action (posing in the sports illustrated swimsuit issue) that increases the attention and scrutiny she's receiving.  it appears she only wants the adulation of positive attention but to be treated with kid gloves when it comes to negative attention.

this kind of issue isn't unique to naomi osaka; every person who is a high profile figure has to deal with increased attention and scrutiny to some degree.  high profile women have the added dimension of often being defined by many men and some women based on their physical attractiveness.  some people desire the attention, others do not.  the people who don't desire the attention in many cases take actions to reduce their visibility, to make themselves less of a target.  they don't change their beliefs one iota, nor do they try to change their personalities, but they are more cautious about what they say and do publicly.

like most of us at one time or another, particularly during our teenage and young adult years, naomi osaka is idealistic, has strong beliefs, but sometimes says or does things without thinking about the consequences of her actions.  most of us are fortunate enough to not be public figures, and therefore don't face heavy scrutiny from thousands of people when we say or do something that is ill-advised or that appears to be contradictory.  but when someone is a high profile public figure who has indicated she has dealt with depression and mental health issues since 2018 (i'm guessing in part because she's been increasingly in the public eye and is uncomfortable with that), she can't expect there to be *no* reaction to her decision to pose in the sports illustrated swimsuit issue, sign on to have a documentary made about her, or agree to have a barbie doll made of her.

i feel like there’s quite a bit of unpacking to do, so i’ll do my best to start you off:

bmi is not a metric for health, and it is not scientifically backed, no matter what the medical community uses it for. it has it’s roots in racism, and when it was created, was never intended to be used for large populations, and certainly was not intended as a measurement of health. i would strongly suggest you look up the origins, learn about how bmi is used in the medical community, and find out how you feel about this on your own. finding a doctor that can have a clear, adult, honest conversation about bmi would be an excellent resource, but if i’m honest, i have found extremely few of those.

beyond that, i would love to understand how one would measure something like “metabolic age,” because the metrics used are what’s really going to really inform you. there isn’t, as far as i know, really a thing called “metabolic age,” in the same way that there isn’t really a thing like… “spinal age.” 

every person, and every body is different. i have a fairly high bmi, but i’m the healthiest i have ever been, and carry much less body fat than i used to. in order for me to reach the “healthy” bmi range for my height, i would have to starve. i’ve actually done that, and i did not look or feel healthy, and had many people asking me if i was “okay,” and if i “needed help buying food.” 

your body and your composition is unique. if you feel healthy, you can do all of the things you want or need to do in your daily life, and are happy with your physique, then i would suggest that there is nothing wrong. chronic illness or other issues like that aside, you are likely perfectly healthy.

please, do not drop your calories down that low. i do not know what your bmr is, but based on my own experimentation, i would expect it would be much higher than 1355 calories per day, and to go below your bmr is a terrible idea.

feeling weak, slow, or having little stamina could be a sign that you are not eating enough. if you want to grow muscle, which is the way that people “look toned,” you *must* eat enough food to grow that muscle. i would tentatively suggest tracking your calories, in order to find out how much you are actually getting, and to see what you need. however, if you have any issues around restriction, hang ups around eating “too much,” or shame around food, i would seriously recommend seeing a therapist first, before embarking on tracking caloric intake. keeping that counsellor around as you start would also be a great idea.

finally, i’ll leave you with this: once, in an effort to make a comfortable fighter jet seat, a massive number of pilots were measured and checked all over. then, the average of those pilots was used to make the seat. not a single pilot felt that the seat was comfortable. not one.

averages do not often work on an individual basis, and should very rarely be applied in such a way.

okay, this is going to sound insane, but please hear me out. i'm going to do my best to be brief and feel free to dm me to further discuss.

throughout life (i'm 28) i've always had minor pain here and there that would come and go, but never anything major or that would stick. i've also never had a major injury in my life.

well out of no where (about 2-3 years ago) i developed bad chronic pain in my shoulder blade region. at first, i thought it was posture based, as i noticed it the most when gaming. but then, i noticed it happening in pretty much any scenario, with no concrete cause. it became debilitating to the point where i was worried gaming and working out (my two most consistent hobbies) would cause permanent damage.

i then saw multiple doctors and eventually ended up in pt. they identified a few "lagging areas" and i did specific exercises for them. i continued to get worse. at the time, i didn't even know that this was possible and they were puzzled. at this point, i was now getting pain down my left arm and tingling in my fingers. i even developed severe lower back pain towards the end. mind you, i went to one of the best pt clinics in my area and they really tried absolutely everything to help me. i was even working directly with the owner at times.

i then decided to reduce my pt appointments to just once a week, and eventually none, as we agreed that there's no reason for me to continue to come in since i was an expert on the exercises and could easily do them at home. my insurance also pulled the plug lol.

i noticed that the less i went to pt and the less i spoke about it/obsessed over it, the better i started to feel (still not great and far from 100%). i tried to be positive and just accept that i can't enjoy my hobbies anymore and just have to move on with life. i didn't mention this earlier on, but i of course got extensive spinal imaging and everything looked great.

right around this time, i accidentally ran into someone else's story that sounded just like mine (he made a youtube video explaining his situation). he explained that proper diagnosis and therapy changed his life and that he had tension myosis syndrome (tms). wikipedia will be your best resource and i've already went into too much detail lol. but essentially, you associate stress with said pain areas and your brain starts to regularly send pain signals to said area(s). the pain is real and is indistinguishable from pain that's due to a structural issue. but, there's of course no underlying issue, just your brain deciding to send stress to that area.

i admittedly didn't follow all of the protocol to treat it, but did my best to understand the treatment in its entirety. the doctor that discovered this has written a few books that people rave about and i wish i got around to reading them. again, read the wiki, but in the simplest of explanations - slowly return to normal life. start doing the things that cause the pain and stick with them as long as the pain is tolerable. continue to ramp up and prove to yourself that the activity (in your case tennis) isn't the issue. a very key part of course is also getting to the bottom of the stress causing it and confronting those issues head on. for me, i was just bottling up too many feelings in my personal life. i started being a lot more upfront with my feelings and opinions towards things and it really was essential to my recovery.

i've gone into far greater detail than i intended, but without ample detail, i sound insane, so wanted to at least set the stage. whenever i hear stories like yours, it kills me, because i know exactly what you're going through. good luck and i hope this helps you!
